item.title: A Bootiful Podcast: 'Data Geekery' with JOOQ creator Lukas Eder
item.dc:creator: joshlong
item.content:encoded:
Hi, Spring fans! In this conversation, Josh Long explores how JOOQ turns SQL into a type-safe, fluent Java language—making complex database work safer, cleaner, and far more expressive. They cover everything from dynamic SQL transformation and cross-dialect support to low-level security, stored procedures, views, and the realities of working with modern databases like DuckDB, ClickHouse, Redshift, and more.

Along the way, Lucas reflects on the origins of JOOQ, why he built it, and how the project has evolved from a clever Java DSL into a serious platform for enterprise-grade database development. The discussion also touches on AI-assisted debugging, the enduring relevance of SQL, and how strong typing can dramatically reduce mental overhead for developers and DBAs alike.

If you care about databases, Java, or writing better software with less friction, this episode is a masterclass in thoughtful engineering and pragmatic elegance.

item.title: Spring AI 2.1 Message Parts: Reasoning That Survives the Round Trip
item.dc:creator: dimitarproynov
item.content:encoded:
Spring AI: Message Parts Doc | Upgrade Notes | OpenAI Responses Doc | Session Doc

Reasoning models do more than think before they answer. They hand part of that thinking back to you and expect to get it back on the next request. Claude signs its thinking blocks. Gemini attaches thought signatures to its function calls. OpenAI's Responses API returns encrypted reasoning items. If you drop, reorder or edit them, the result ranges from an HTTP 400 to a model that quietly loses its earlier reasoning and starts over.

Until now, a Spring AI message was a piece of text with side lists of tool calls and media. There was no place for that data, let alone its order. Spring AI 2.1 changes the data model itself: every message now holds its content as an ordered list of message parts. A part is one piece of a response, such as a run of text, a block of reasoning or a tool call. Providers call these pieces content blocks (Anthropic, Bedrock), parts (Gemini), items (OpenAI Responses) or chunks (Mistral), and Spring AI maps them all to message parts.

With the 2.1.0-RC1 release candidate, the major chat models produce and consume parts: OpenAI Responses, Anthropic, Google GenAI, OpenAI Chat Completions, Ollama, Bedrock Converse, DeepSeek and Mistral AI. The release also adds Session memory, which persists them. This post covers the new abstraction, why the Responses API needed it, and what each chat model gains. It comes down to three rules: keep the order, replay what you were given verbatim, and persist the parts, not the text.

Why a String Was Not Enough

Here is what Claude, with thinking enabled, returns in a single tool-calling round:

thinking   "The user wants the weather in Paris. I should call get_weather..."   signature: "EqQBCgIYAhIM..."
text       "Let me check that for you."
tool_use   get_weather {"location": "Paris"}

When you send the tool result, Anthropic wants this turn back exactly as it was: same blocks, same order, signature included. Before 2.1, AssistantMessage could not do that:

  1. No order across kinds. Text, tool calls and media lived in separate fields, so replay had to guess an order.
  2. No home for opaque data. Signatures and encrypted reasoning are opaque: the client cannot read them and must send them back unchanged. They sat under provider-specific metadata keys or in package-private subclasses.
  3. Streaming lost it. The aggregator merged chunk metadata key by key, so thinking often survived only as its last fragment.
  4. Memory lost it. JdbcChatMemoryRepository stores only the text and the message type.

The MessagePart Abstraction

AbstractMessage now holds a parts: List<MessagePart>, shared by every message type:

MessagePart is a sealed interface with six record implementations:

Part Holds Used for
TextPart a run of text answers, prompts
ReasoningPart reasoning text, an optional summary, an optional payload Claude thinking, Gemini thoughts, DeepSeek reasoning_content
ToolCallPart an AssistantMessage.ToolCall, an optional payload function calls
ToolResultPart a tool result whose content is a list of other MessageParts tool results carrying more than text
MediaPart a Media: image, audio, video, document multimodal input and output
UnknownPart the raw JSON of a block Spring AI does not model server tool calls, citations, code execution

Adding MessagePart achieves:

  • Order is data. Parts keep the order the provider produced them in, so a thinking block stays in front of the tool call it led to.
  • Opaque payloads are replayed, never interpreted. A part can carry an OpaquePayload(provider, kind, data), such as an Anthropic signature, a Gemini thought_signature or an OpenAI encrypted_content. The ChatModel that produced it sends it back unchanged, and every other chat model skips it. This keeps a history safe to move between providers.
  • Nothing is dropped silently. A block a ChatModel does not understand becomes an UnknownPart and is replayed as-is to the provider that produced it.

The change is backward compatible. Constructors and builder methods keep working and produce parts in the order 2.0 used: text, tool calls, media. getText(), getToolCalls() and getMedia() are now views over the parts, next to the new getReasoning(), and getParts() returns everything in order. Code that reads reasoning is what most likely needs an update, since each chat model exposed it differently before 2.1:

ChatResponse response = chatModel.call(prompt);

// Before 2.1: each chat model exposed reasoning its own way
List<String> thoughts = response.getResults().stream()              // Google GenAI
    .filter(g -> Boolean.TRUE.equals(g.getOutput().getMetadata().get("isThought")))
    .map(g -> g.getOutput().getText())
    .toList();
String reasoning = ((DeepSeekAssistantMessage) response.getResult().getOutput())
    .getReasoningContent();                                          // DeepSeek

// 2.1: one accessor for every chat model
List<String> thoughts = response.getResult().getOutput().getReasoning().stream()
    .map(ReasoningPart::text)
    .toList();
String answer = response.getResult().getOutput().getText();          // unchanged

The upgrade notes list the remaining changes per chat model. When streaming, each part is stamped with its content block index and a partial flag, and MessageAggregator merges the deltas. The aggregated message equals the one a blocking call returns, signature included.

How Message Parts Made the Responses API Possible

Spring AI implements two OpenAI chat model endpoints. OpenAiChatModel uses Chat Completions, OpenAI's original chat API, which many other servers also implement. OpenAiResponsesChatModel, new in 2.1, uses the Responses API, OpenAI's newer API for reasoning models and agents, in its stateless mode.

The Responses API does not return a message. Each call returns an output array of items: reasoning, function_call and message, plus items for the tools OpenAI runs itself, such as web search. Each reasoning item carries its own id and encrypted_content.

OpenAiResponsesChatModel is stateless by design: it does not keep the conversation on OpenAI's side, but replays all of it on every call, so memory, advisors and RAG work exactly as they do with OpenAiChatModel. For a reasoning model, the replay works well only if it includes the model's earlier reasoning. OpenAI's reasoning guide asks for the reasoning items, function calls and function call outputs since the last user message.

Before 2.1, AssistantMessage could not hold these items faithfully:

  • It had no way to say "reasoning, then function call, then message".
  • It could not attach data to a single item. Each reasoning item has an id and carries the model's reasoning in encrypted form (encrypted_content), and both have to be sent back with that item. A message had only one metadata map for the whole response.
  • It had nowhere to keep the items of tools OpenAI runs itself, such as web search, without faking them as local tool calls.

With parts, the mapping is one to one and keeps the order of the output array:

Responses API item Message part
reasoning ReasoningPart with the summary, OpaquePayload("openai.responses", "encrypted_content", …) and the item id
function_call ToolCallPart with the item id
message TextPart
image_generation_call MediaPart
web search, file search, code interpreter, MCP, any other item UnknownPart with the raw JSON

On the next request, the chat model rebuilds the input items from the parts in the same order. That replay is worth having. OpenAI's now archived cookbook on better performance from reasoning models reports that including reasoning items "led to about a 3% improvement" on SWE-bench. Responses is also the endpoint for agents on current OpenAI models. Starting with GPT-5.4, Chat Completions does not support tool calling with a reasoning effort other than none.

What Each Chat Model Gains

Every other chat model follows the same pattern: map each response block to one part, rebuild the request from the parts in order, and replay only its own payloads. What that buys depends on what each provider demands:

Chat model Now replayed Improvement
Anthropic signed and redacted thinking, in block order; server tool blocks tool turns Claude accepts, reasoning continuity, cache hits
Google GenAI each thought signature on the part that carried it no errors on Gemini 3+ function calls, full reasoning quality on other parts
OpenAI Chat Completions reasoning_content continuity on vLLM, gpt-oss, Kimi and other compatible servers
Ollama the thinking field continuity in gpt-oss and qwen3 tool loops
Bedrock Converse signed, redacted and unsigned reasoning, also when streaming streaming tool loops with extended thinking work
DeepSeek reasoning_content of streamed and restored messages no errors in thinking mode with tools
Mistral AI thinking chunks, in chunk order the output quality Mistral says is lost without them

Anthropic

Within a tool-use turn, Claude requires its thinking blocks back, and you "can't rearrange, edit, or partially drop them": modified blocks are rejected with an HTTP 400. Before 2.1, Spring AI rebuilt the turn as text, then thinking, then tool use, whatever order Claude had used. It also dropped server tool blocks, and the streamed thinking never fully reached the aggregated message. Now every block is one part, replayed in order with its signature. Anthropic names two more gains: preserved thinking "lets Claude continue reasoning from where it left off", and preserved thinking blocks "enable cache hits during tool use". Claude Opus 4.5 and later, and Sonnet 4.6 and later, also keep earlier turns' thinking in context, which is where Session memory comes in.

Google GenAI

Google's thought signatures guide says to return each signature "in the exact part where it was received". On Gemini 3 and later, a missing signature on a function call fails the request "with a 400 error". On other parts, "performance may degrade". Spring AI previously collected all signatures in one list and reattached them to function calls by position. It also dropped the thoughts and text in front of a function call from the tool loop. Now each signature travels on its own part, and code execution and server-side tool parts are sent back as received.

OpenAI Chat Completions

OpenAI's own Chat Completions API returns no reasoning text, so Responses should be used for OpenAI reasoning models. OpenAiChatModel serves the compatible servers that do return reasoning_content, such as vLLM, gpt-oss deployments and Kimi. OpenAI's harmony guide asks you to pass gpt-oss's chain of thought back during tool calling. That replay already existed in 2.0.x, through a metadata key. It now rides on parts, so it survives persistence. Reasoning signed by another provider is never forwarded, and for servers that reject the field there is replayReasoningContent(false).

Ollama

Before 2.1, thinking lived only in response metadata and was never sent back. When streaming, only its last fragment survived. Now it is replayed in the assistant message's thinking field, as Ollama's tool calling docs ask: "return those fields together with any tool results in the follow-up request". The gain depends on the model. The gpt-oss and qwen3 templates use the reasoning of the current tool loop.

Bedrock Converse

Bedrock applies the Claude rule: "During tool use, you must pass thinking blocks back to the API for the last assistant message". BedrockProxyChatModel previously dropped reasoning from streamed responses. Now a response is a single generation of parts in block order, streams carry the reasoning, the signature and redacted reasoning, and unsigned reasoning from gpt-oss is replayed too.

DeepSeek

In thinking mode, a request that carries tools must pass back the reasoning_content of earlier assistant messages, or the API returns a 400. Before 2.1, Spring AI sent it only for DeepSeekAssistantMessage instances, so streamed responses and messages restored from memory went out without it. Now any assistant message replays its ReasoningParts, streamed or not, and DeepSeekAssistantMessage is deprecated.

Mistral AI

Mistral's reasoning docs say: "always replay the full assistant message (including ThinkChunk)". They warn that dropping the reasoning trace "degrades model performance". Before 2.1, MistralAiChatModel never sent thinking back. Now thinking, text, citation and image chunks become parts and are replayed in chunk order, including between the rounds of a tool loop.

Memory That Keeps the Parts: Spring AI Session

Replay inside one ChatClient call is half the story. Between calls, the history lives in chat memory, and of the ChatMemory repositories only the in-memory one keeps the parts. With any other, the model reasons from scratch on each restored turn.

Spring AI Session, now part of Spring AI 2.1, closes that gap. A session is an append-only event log. Each message is stored as its full list of parts, payloads and attributes included, and the JDBC store keeps them as JSON. JdbcChatMemoryRepository, the JDBC store behind ChatMemory, keeps only the text and drops tool calls and tool results entirely. Two more properties matter for reasoning models:

  • Every tool round is recorded. SessionMemoryAdvisor runs inside the tool-calling loop, so it stores each round's tool calls and results, not just the final answer. Each round's prompt is rebuilt from the session, so signatures make the round trip through the store.
  • Compaction respects turns. When the history is trimmed or summarized, the cut always lands on a turn boundary. A tool call never loses its result, and the reasoning in front of it stays with it.

Add the spring-ai-starter-model-session-jdbc starter, register the session advisors and pass a session id on each call:

@Bean
ChatClient chatClient(ChatClient.Builder builder, SessionService sessionService) {
    return builder
        .defaultAdvisors(SessionAdvisors.builder(sessionService)
            .compaction(new TurnCountTrigger(20),
                    WindowCompactionStrategy.builder().lastTurns(10).build())
            .build())
        .build();
}

String answer = chatClient.prompt()
    .user("Find the cheapest flight to Lisbon next Friday")
    .advisors(SessionAdvisors.session("session-42"))
    .call()
    .content();

With this in place, the gains above carry across calls and restarts. Claude still sees its earlier thinking, Gemini gets each signature back on the right part, and DeepSeek's thinking-mode rule holds after a redeploy. ChatMemory and its repositories are deprecated in 2.1 and will be removed in 3.0.0. The migration guide maps one API onto the other.

?? Things to know

One generation per response. Before 2.1, Anthropic, Google GenAI and Bedrock Converse split a response into separate Generations for thinking, tool calls and text. They now return one per candidate. Read reasoning with getResult().getOutput().getReasoning().

Histories stored before 2.1 have no reasoning parts. Messages that an earlier version wrote to chat memory come back without their reasoning, so it is not replayed.

Cross-provider history is safe, not lossless. Reasoning signed by one provider is never sent to another. When you switch models mid-conversation, the text and tool calls carry over, but the other vendor's reasoning does not.

Keep part attributes. Mistral, and Bedrock for unsigned reasoning, replay reasoning only when the part's provider attribute names them. If you store history yourself, don't strip attributes.

Conclusion

Message parts turn a Spring AI message from a string with attachments into a faithful record of what the model produced and in what order. The key insights:

  • Order is part of the data. Reasoning models check the order and integrity of what you send back. A string with side lists can carry neither.
  • Replay what you were given, verbatim. OpaquePayload lets each chat model return its own signatures unchanged and skip everyone else's.
  • Persist the parts, not the text. Session memory stores every part of every tool round, so reasoning survives across calls and restarts.

Resources

Spring AI

  • Message Parts and Upgrading to 2.1.0, with per-provider changes
  • OpenAI Responses
  • Session memory and Migrating to Session Memory

Related Spring AI articles

  • Spring AI Agentic Patterns (Part 7): Session API

item.title: Using Your Own Embeddings in Spring AI 2.1
item.dc:creator: sobychacko
item.content:encoded:
VectorStore.add() takes text documents, generates embeddings with the store's configured model, and saves both. Spring AI 2.1 adds upsert for applications that already have embeddings or generate them from images, video, or audio. It accepts documents paired with application-supplied vectors, without calling the store's embedding model. A new similaritySearch overload also accepts a query embedding, giving applications control over both indexing and searching.

When to supply your own embeddings

Let's look at a real-world example. Consider a furniture catalog with a product listed as "Armchair, model A42". Its photo shows green velvet upholstery and wooden legs, but a search for "green velvet armchair" could miss it if those details are absent from the description.

A multimodal embedding model produces image and text embeddings that can be compared directly, letting the search match the customer's words to the photo. The application stores photo embeddings with upsert, then embeds search text with the same model to find the closest matches.

Video or audio search works similarly if the model supports comparing that content with text queries. For example, store an embedding for a training video segment about replacing a filter (04:00 to 04:30), with the video URL and start and end times in metadata. A search for "how to replace the filter" can then return a result that the application opens at 04:00.

Existing text embeddings benefit too, whether they come from a provider's batch API, another team, or a database migration. add() would generate them again. Writing directly to the database avoids that, but requires matching Spring AI's field names and formats for IDs, text, metadata, and vectors so it can read and search the records. upsert handles that storage format for you.

Indexing product images

For the furniture catalog, let's assume that we are using Spring AI's VertexAiMultimodalEmbeddingModel, which supports text, images, and video. The examples below use these two fields:

private final VertexAiMultimodalEmbeddingModel multimodal;

private final VectorStore vectorStore;

First, we generate an embedding for a product photo and pair it with the document we want to store:

Document photo = Document.builder()
    .media(new Media(MimeTypeUtils.IMAGE_JPEG, product.photo()))
    .build();
float[] vector = this.multimodal.call(new DocumentEmbeddingRequest(photo)).getResult().getOutput();

Document row = Document.builder()
    .id(UUID.nameUUIDFromBytes(product.sku().getBytes(UTF_8)).toString())
    .text("")
    .metadata(DocumentMetadata.CONTENT_REF.value(), product.photoUrl())
    .metadata("sku", product.sku())
    .metadata("inStock", product.inStock())
    .build();

this.vectorStore.upsert(List.of(new EmbeddedDocument(row, vector)));

photo carries the image sent to the model; row holds the product metadata and photo reference. EmbeddedDocument pairs row with the image embedding (the vector).

Document requires text or media. Current vector store implementations persist an ID, text, metadata, and a vector, and use those fields to reconstruct search results. They reject media documents such as photo because they cannot persist its media content. Using .text("") above keeps row valid while the photo stays in external storage; upsert never embeds that empty text. A product description in .text(...) would be saved and returned with search results, but upsert would still use the supplied image embedding without embedding the description.

DocumentMetadata.CONTENT_REF holds the photo's URL in metadata. The application uses it to display search results; Spring AI does not fetch the photo.

Before running this example, make sure the vector store's dimensions match the model's output. For 1408-dimensional embeddings, for example, set PGvector's spring.ai.vectorstore.pgvector.dimensions=1408, or use dimensions(1408) on its builder. An existing table's vector column must also have a compatible dimension.

Searching with a query embedding

Embed the customer's search text with the same multimodal model:

float[] query = this.multimodal.call(new DocumentEmbeddingRequest(new Document("green velvet armchair")))
    .getResult()
    .getOutput();

List<Document> chairs = this.vectorStore.similaritySearch(query,
        SearchRequest.builder().topK(12).filterExpression("inStock == true").build());

similaritySearch(float[], SearchRequest) uses the supplied vector without calling the store's embedding model. The request controls topK, the similarity threshold, and metadata filters; any query text is ignored.

Generate the product image and query text embeddings with a model designed to compare images and text. Using an unrelated model for queries can produce meaningless results, even if its embeddings have the same number of dimensions. Keep this in mind when using the overload that accepts query text: it uses the store's configured embedding model.

Follow the model's recommended input settings for indexing content and embedding queries; using the wrong setting can reduce search relevance. If you later change models, you may need to regenerate stored embeddings. Keeping the model name and version in metadata helps identify which documents need updating.

Updating existing documents

upsert inserts documents with new IDs and replaces those with existing IDs, so stable IDs derived from product SKUs, as in the example above, let the indexing job update photos without creating duplicates. This replacement contract applies to every supporting store; with add(), behavior for repeated IDs depends on the store.

Each upsert call accepts a list of documents paired with their embeddings. An empty list returns without writing anything. Writes within a single call are not guaranteed to be transactional: if one fails, the call throws an exception, but some documents may already have been written. After resolving the cause, retry the entire list with the same IDs and input.

Vector validation

EmbeddedDocument rejects empty vectors and non-finite values (NaN or infinity) at construction. When the store knows its index dimension, it checks every vector in the list before writing, so a mismatch prevents any writes. These checks cannot detect incompatible embedding spaces.

Spring AI gets the expected vector size from configuration or by reading the existing index, table, or collection. The embedding model is consulted for dimensions only when creating an index without an explicit size.

If Spring AI cannot read the index's expected vector size and none is configured, stores other than Redis still send the vectors to the database, which applies its own size checks. Spring AI tries to read the expected size again on the next call.

Redis can save a vector of the wrong size without reporting an error, but that document will not appear in vector search results. To prevent this, RedisVectorStore throws before writing when it cannot determine the expected size. Configure dimensions to match the Redis index, or make sure the index exists and is readable, then retry.

Vector store support

VectorStore.upsert(List<EmbeddedDocument>) and VectorStoreRetriever.similaritySearch(float[], SearchRequest) are opt-in default methods that throw UnsupportedOperationException until implemented. Existing store implementations continue to compile.

As of Spring AI 2.1.0-RC1, PGvector, Redis, Elasticsearch, Qdrant, and OpenSearch support both upsert and searching with a query embedding.

For stores extending AbstractObservationVectorStore, implement doUpsert and doSimilaritySearch(float[], SearchRequest), and override supportsUpsert() and supportsQueryEmbeddingSearch() to return true. The base class checks support before creating observations and records upsert as a separate operation in vector store metrics.

Existing applications can continue using add() to have the store generate embeddings for text documents.

Getting started

For more details, see the reference documentation on writing your own embeddings and searching with a query embedding. Thanks to Aniket Gupta, whose proposal in #3541 started this work.

Try these APIs and share feedback through GitHub issues.

item.title: This Week in Spring - October 27th, 2026
item.dc:creator: joshlong
item.content:encoded:
Hi, Spring fans! Welcome to another installment of This Week in Spring, which I write from the paradise-like environs Barcelona, Spain, where I was lucky enough to be a part of the amazing Vaadin Create event today and tomorrow. It's been an amazing few days, but those few days are just a small part of the week, and what a week it's been! Let's dive into the the weekly roundup!

  • yet another amazing post from Craig Walls in his ongoing series looking at Spring Ai - Speeding Up RAG with Faster Embeddings
  • and another one (DJ Khalid!): Rendering Rich UIs with MCP Apps
  • I am so curious about the wide and wonderful world of agentic development these days. I was especially keen on learning how Netflix made AI coding agents more efficient with JetBrains IDE intelligence
  • speaking of JetBrains, I was overjoyed to talk to JetBrains' Anton Arhipov last week about the amazing world of AI Development with JetBrains IDEs in A Bootiful Podcast.
  • did u every want to add a reasoning model to your Spring Boot application as a plain Mavend dependency? Well, now you can with Quixotic AI
